Chichester
chich'ess-ter
n. (cathedral city of Sussex; a see that changed hands with every change of crown between 1543 and 1570)
From Old English Cissanceaster, the fort of Cissa, on the Roman Noviomagus; ceaster, a walled town.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Chichester shows what the English Reformation looked like from a provincial see. George Day was made bishop in 1543, was deprived under Edward VI in 1551 for refusing to replace the stone altars with tables, was restored by Mary in 1553 and died in office in 1556; John Scory, an Edwardian who had fled abroad under Mary and conformed briefly on his return, was translated to Hereford; William Barlow, who had already changed his position more than once under Henry, held the see from 1559. Within twenty-seven years the diocese had four bishops of three different convictions, and its clergy and people were required to follow each. The dictionary records the see because such a sequence produces the condition Paul names and warns against: men “tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine” (Eph 4:14).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines to deprive as to divest of office or dignity; to waver as to fluctuate in opinion, to be undetermined; and stedfastness as firmness, fixedness in principle.

expand to see more

DEPRIVE, v.t. [L. deprivo.] To take from; to divest of office or dignity; to depose; to divest of an ecclesiastical preferment.

WAVER, v.i. To play or move to and fro; to fluctuate in opinion; to be undetermined; to be unsettled.

STEDFASTNESS, n. Firmness; fixedness in place or principle; constancy; resolution.

SLEIGHT, n. An artful trick; sly artifice; dexterous practice; cunning.

Key Scripture

Eph 4:14 — "That we henceforth be no more children, tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine, by the sleight of men, and cunning craftiness, whereby they lie in wait to deceive;"

Jam 1:6 — "But let him ask in faith, nothing wavering. For he that wavereth is like a wave of the sea driven with the wind and tossed."

Heb 13:9 — "Be not carried about with divers and strange doctrines. For it is a good thing that the heart be established with grace; not with meats, which have not profited them that have been occupied therein."

2Pe 3:17 — "Ye therefore, beloved, seeing ye know these things before, beware lest ye also, being led away with the error of the wicked, fall from your own stedfastness."

Modern Corruption

Four bishops of three convictions in twenty-seven years, as the Sussex see changed hands with Henry, Edward, Mary and Elizabeth.

expand to see more

The corruption to name is the one the Tudor settlement made almost unavoidable: the belief that the doctrine of a diocese is whatever the current sovereign requires, and the career clergy that belief produces. William Barlow held four English sees under three monarchs and signed for each of them. The dictionary does not treat every conforming minister as a hypocrite, since some genuinely changed their minds and some judged that staying served their people better than leaving; but a church in which the ordinary way to keep a bishopric is to change doctrine twice has a problem the change of sovereign did not cause.

The principle to recover is stability of doctrine and the settling of the heart by grace rather than by authority. James describes the unstable man as “a wave of the sea driven with the wind and tossed” (Jam 1:6). Hebrews gives both the warning and the remedy: “Be not carried about with divers and strange doctrines. For it is a good thing that the heart be established with grace” (Heb 13:9). And Peter warns those who have been forewarned, to “beware lest ye also, being led away with the error of the wicked, fall from your own stedfastness” (2Pe 3:17).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek kludonizomai (G2831), to be tossed as by waves; Greek sterigmos (G4740), stedfastness.

expand to see more

Greek kludonizomai (G2831) — to be tossed by waves, to fluctuate; Ephesians 4:14.

Greek sterigmos (G4740) — firmness, stedfastness, a fixed position; 2 Peter 3:17.

Greek kubeia (G2940) — dice-playing, and so sleight, trickery; Ephesians 4:14.

Greek diakrino (G1252) — to waver, to doubt, to be divided; James 1:6.

Greek bebaioo (G950) — to confirm, to establish; Hebrews 13:9.

Usage

"“tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine” (Eph 4:14) — four bishops in twenty-seven years."

"“Be not carried about with divers and strange doctrines. For it is a good thing that the heart be established with grace” (Heb 13:9) — George Day deprived in 1551 and restored in 1553."

"“beware lest ye also, being led away with the error of the wicked, fall from your own stedfastness” (2Pe 3:17) — William Barlow held four English sees under three monarchs."
